final_answer:
>>> When an mRNA vaccine is injected into the body, it is delivered into muscle cells via lipid nanoparticles that protect the mRNA from degradation.  
>>> The lipid nanoparticles fuse with the cell membrane, releasing the mRNA into the cytoplasm of the cell.  
>>> The cell’s ribosomes read the mRNA sequence and use it as a blueprint to produce viral proteins (e.g., the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2).  
>>> These proteins are displayed on the cell surface or secreted into the surrounding tissue, acting as antigens.  
>>> The immune system detects these foreign proteins, activating B cells and T cells. B cells produce antibodies specific to the viral protein, while T cells target and destroy infected cells.  
>>> After the mRNA is used to synthesize the protein, it is degraded by the cell, and the immune response subsides.  
>>> Memory B and T cells remain in the body, enabling a rapid and robust response if the actual virus is encountered later.  
>>> This process generates immunity without causing infection, as the mRNA does not integrate into the genome or replicate.
